project.name: Medical Device
project.description: This model shows how medical data moves between devices, patient apps, cloud services, and clinicians across secure boundaries.

components.description: Physical hardware interacting with the patient.

components.description: Input store or buffer holding raw physiological measurements from sensors.

components.name: Health Controller
components.description: Core processing logic that interprets sensor data and manages device state.

components.name: Operating System
components.description: Embedded firmware/OS managing hardware resources and communications.

components.name: Clinician Services

components.name: Medical Data

components.name: Clinician

threats.name: App Proxy Attack
threats.description:
Attacker uses an on phone app to proxy attacks against the medical app.

Attacker goal / impact: Interception: Inspect/modify traffic via local proxy.

threats.name: Broken access control
threats.description:
An attacker could exploit broken access control to access unauthorized functionality and data, such as accessing other users' accounts, viewing sensitive files, modifying other users’ data, and changing access rights.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Unauthorized viewing/modifying data.

threats.name: Broken Authentication
threats.description:
Attackers could target authentication mechanisms, potentially gaining complete control of other users' accounts, accessing their data, and performing actions on their behalf.

Attacker goal / impact: Account Takeover: Hijack user sessions.

threats.name: Broken Function Level Authorization
threats.description:
An attacker could send legitimate API calls to endpoints they should not have access to, leading to unauthorized access to functionality and potentially service disruption.

Attacker goal / impact: Privilege Esc: User accesses Admin/Clinician APIs.

threats.name: Broken Object Level Authorization
threats.description:
An attacker could exploit API endpoints with broken object-level authorization by manipulating the object ID in the request, leading to unauthorized access to data.

Attacker goal / impact: Data Breach: Access other patients' records (BOLA/IDOR).

threats.name: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
threats.description:
An attacker could access private/sensitive object properties, potentially leading to data disclosure, corruption, or unauthorized privilege escalation.

Attacker goal / impact: Data Breach: View hidden sensitive fields (Mass Assignment).

threats.name: Bypass Access Control
threats.description:
As an attacker, I aim to bypass access control checks by modifying the URL via parameter tampering or force browsing, altering the internal application state, manipulating the HTML page, or using specialized attack tools to modify API requests.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Force browsing to hidden URLs.

threats.name: Client-Side Injection
threats.description:
Attackers exploit vulnerabilities by injecting malicious code (e.g., JavaScript, SQL queries) into the mobile app.

Attacker goal / impact: Code Exec: Run malicious JS or SQL on the phone.

threats.name: Credential Leakage
threats.description:
Secrets such as API keys, tokens, or credentials could be accidentally exposed in logs or code.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Keys/Secrets found in GitHub/Logs.

threats.name: Cryptographic failure
threats.description:
An attacker could exploit cryptographic failures to access sensitive data unprotected, such as credit card information, personal data, or business secrets.

Attacker goal / impact: Exposure: Weak encryption (MD5) or bad keys.

threats.name: Data Disclosure
threats.description:
Excessively collecting, storing, processing, or sharing personal data. The data minimization principle is critical here: only the strictly necessary data should be collected or disclosed. Data disclosure can be explicit, i.e., intended or designed by the system, or implicit, i.e., unintended or indirect (e.g., through metadata or derived from other data). The focus is on four threat characteristics: Unnecessary data types: this relates to the data type sensitivity, granularity, and encoding, which can be too detailed Excessive data volume: this relates to the amount and frequency of the data processing and the number of involved data subjects, which can be too high Unnecessary processing: this relates to the further data treatment analysis, propagation, or retention, which can be considered not strictly necessary Excessive exposure: this relates to the different parties with whom the data is shared, which can be considered too much, and how widely accessible the data is

Attacker goal / impact: Privacy Breach: Exposing PII/PHI unnecessarily.

threats.name: Data exfiltration from local storage
threats.description:
Sensitive patient data and device telemetry stored on the device (e.g., logs, cached PHI, configuration files, or database files) can be read and copied by an attacker with local or logical access. An adversary who gains physical access, exploits a local service vulnerability, or abuses exposed interfaces (USB, removable media, debug ports, or unsecured APIs) can extract PHI or intellectual property and transfer it off-device, leading to privacy breaches, regulatory violations, and targeted follow-on attacks.

Attacker goal / impact: Theft: Copying DB files from device.

threats.name: Denial of Service
threats.description:
Denial of service (DoS) is an attack that disrupts the normal functioning of a system or network by overwhelming it with excessive traffic or requests.

Attacker goal / impact: Availability: System offline.

threats.name: Denial-of-therapy or over-therapy due to cyber event
threats.description:
A cyberattack or system failure causes the medical device to stop, delay, or excessively deliver therapy—such as halting an infusion pump, disabling pacing, or continuously delivering stimulation—resulting in potential patient harm or device damage.

Attacker goal / impact: Patient Safety: Stop or overdose therapy (e.g., insulin/pacing).

threats.name: Detecting
threats.description:
Deducing the involvement of an individual by observing. Detecting threats does not require being able to read the actual data – merely knowing that the data exists, is sufficient to infer more (sensitive) information. Detecting can be done through observed communications: the communication to a system or service, or between different systems can be observed, observed application side-effects: actions in an application have side-effects that can be observed. E.g., temporary files in the file system, and evoked system responses: the system leaks the existence of certain data through its responses. These threats also relate to linking and identifying, as the deduced info can be used to extract more info on an individual.

Attacker goal / impact: Inference: Deducing medical condition by observation.

threats.name: Elevation of Privilege
threats.description:
Elevation of privilege is when an attacker gains unauthorized access to higher-level permissions or rights within a system or application.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Gaining Root/Admin rights.

threats.name: Hard-coded Credentials
threats.description:
The product contains hard-coded credentials, such as a password or cryptographic key, which it uses for its inbound authentication, outbound communication to external components, or encryption of internal data.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Backdoor via static password/keys.

threats.name: Hidden debug or maintenance interfaces
threats.description:
The device includes hardware or software service interfaces (e.g., UART, JTAG, USB serial, or proprietary maintenance modes) intended for manufacturing, calibration, or servicing. If these interfaces remain accessible, undocumented, or insufficiently protected in the production environment, an attacker with physical or insider access could exploit them to gain unauthorized control of the device.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Bypass auth via exposed hardware ports.

threats.name: Identification and Authentication Failures
threats.description:
An attacker could exploit identification and authentication failures to impersonate legitimate users and gain unauthorized system access.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Impersonation of legitimate users.

threats.name: Identifying
threats.description:
Learning the identity of an individual. Although many systems require the identification of data subjects, identifying threats arise when the identity can be revealed through leaks, deduction, or inference in cases where this is not intentional or desired. Identifying can be done through Identified data when the system explicitly maintains the link to the identity or refers to the identity (e.g., in the metadata). Identifiable data: The identity can be derived indirectly, e.g., from pseudonyms, identity-revealing content, or through a small anonymity set. Identifying threats is also related to linking. (Re-)identification can also result in unawareness and non-compliance issues.

Attacker goal / impact: De-anonymization: Learning user identity from data.

threats.name: Improper Inventory Management
threats.description:
Attackers could gain unauthorized access through old API versions, unpatched endpoints, or third parties with weaker security, leading to data leaks or server takeover.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Attackers exploit old/unpatched API versions.

threats.name: Improper Memory Buffer Restriction
threats.description:
The product performs operations on a memory buffer, but an attacker can read from or write to a memory location outside the buffer's intended boundary.

Attacker goal / impact: Exploit: Buffer overflow leading to code execution.

threats.name: Information Disclosure
threats.description:
Information disclosure is the unintentional exposure or release of confidential or sensitive data to unauthorized individuals or entities.

Attacker goal / impact: Leakage: General exposure of system info.

threats.name: Injection flaws
threats.description:
An attacker could use injection flaws (like SQL, NoSQL, and OS command injection) to send hostile data to an interpreter, leading to data loss, corruption, lack of accountability, or denial of access. With SQL injection, without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data. This can be used to alter query logic to bypass security checks or to insert additional statements that modify the back-end database, possibly including the execution of system commands. SQL injection has become a common issue with database-driven websites. The flaw is easily detected and easily exploited. As such, any site or product package with even a minimal user base is likely to be subject to an attempted attack of this kind. This flaw depends on the fact that SQL makes no real distinction between the control and data planes.

Attacker goal / impact: Database Compromise: SQL/Command Injection.

threats.name: Insecure boot
threats.description:
Without a secure boot chain (root of trust → authenticated bootloader → signed firmware → measured OS), the device cannot cryptographically guarantee that only vendor-approved code runs at boot. This enables attackers to replace or modify firmware, implant persistent rootkits in early-boot stages, bypass higher-level software protections, and evade detection by tampering with logging or attestation mechanisms.

Attacker goal / impact: Control: Run malicious firmware/rootkit (Lack of Root of Trust).

threats.name: Insecure Communication with Third-Party Services
threats.description:
Mobile apps often interact with third-party APIs or services, which may be insecure or malicious.

Attacker goal / impact: Leakage: Data sent to insecure ad/analytics APIs.

threats.name: Insecure Data Storage
threats.description:
Sensitive data (like personal information, credentials, or financial data) stored insecurely on the device can be accessed by unauthorized parties if the device is lost, stolen, or compromised.

Attacker goal / impact: Data Theft: Read PHI from unencrypted local files.

threats.name: Insecure firmware update mechanism
threats.description:
The device accepts firmware updates without properly verifying authenticity, integrity, or authorization of the update package or the update source.

Attacker goal / impact: Control: Flash malicious OS to device.

threats.name: Insecure Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
threats.description:
Insecure communication between apps or components can be intercepted or manipulated.

Attacker goal / impact: Leakage: Malicious apps read medical app data.

threats.name: Insufficient Transport Layer Protection
threats.description:
Data transmitted between the mobile app and server can be intercepted if not properly encrypted.

Attacker goal / impact: Interception: HTTP instead of HTTPS/TLS.

threats.name: Least Privilege Principle Violation
threats.description:
An attacker breaches the deny-by-default policy, leading to potential exploitation, data breaches, or unauthorized control over system functionalities.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Users have too many rights.

threats.name: Linking
threats.description:
Associating data items or user actions to learn more about an individual or a group. Linking may lead to unwanted privacy implications, even if it does not reveal one's identity. Data items or user actions can be linked through identifiers: a username, IP address, phone model, sensor type, the combination of data items or sets: a browser fingerprint, location trace profiling, derivation, or inference, and group profiling is a form of linking. In that case, data on a group of individuals is combined in a way that may negatively impact privacy, e.g., through extensive profiling, recommendations, etc. Linking can also lead to identifying, detecting, and non-repudiation threats. Data disclosure threats trigger linking: the more data is available, the more likely linking threats occur.

Attacker goal / impact: Re-identification: Correlating data to identify user.

threats.name: Logging Failure
threats.description:
An attacker can attack the App Server, and because it does not log at the correct level, the Response team is unaware of the attack.​

Attacker goal / impact: Blindness: No forensic trail of attacks.

threats.name: Logic flaws in control software that could alter therapy or diagnosis
threats.description:
Defects or design errors in the device’s control logic can cause incorrect operation of therapeutic or diagnostic functions. An attacker or unintended condition could trigger these flaws to alter dosage, measurement, or timing—resulting in inaccurate diagnosis, inappropriate therapy delivery, or patient harm.

Attacker goal / impact: Patient Safety: Trigger edge-case bugs to alter therapy.

threats.name: M1: Improper Credential Usage
threats.description:
Apps store or handle credentials insecurely (e.g., plaintext storage, hardcoded secrets, weak tokens). Attackers can extract or reuse credentials to impersonate users or access backend systems.

Attacker goal / impact: Account Takeover: Hardcoded/weak tokens in app code.

threats.name: M2: Inadequate Supply Chain Security
threats.description:
Third-party SDKs, libraries, or build pipelines are compromised or unverified. Malicious components introduce backdoors or data-leakage paths into otherwise secure mobile apps.

Attacker goal / impact: Backdoor: Compromised SDK/Library in app.

threats.name: M6: Inadequate Privacy Controls
threats.description:
Apps over-collect, mishandle, or expose personal and health data. Unauthorized analytics or storage leaks can result in privacy violations and regulatory non-compliance (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR).

Attacker goal / impact: Compliance: App over-collects PII or leaks to analytics.

threats.name: M7: Insufficient Binary Protections
threats.description:
Lack of code obfuscation, anti-debugging, or integrity checks allows reverse engineering. Attackers extract keys, modify app logic, or repackage trojanized versions.

Attacker goal / impact: Cloning: App is easily decompiled/tampered.

threats.name: Malicious Code and Malware
threats.description:
Mobile devices can be infected with malware that can compromise apps, steal data, or perform unauthorized actions.

Attacker goal / impact: Control: Phone malware captures keystrokes/screen.

threats.name: Medical Social Engineering
threats.description:
An adversary uses deception (phishing, vishing, pretexting, or impersonation) targeted at clinicians, patients, or support staff to trick them into revealing credentials, approving unsafe configuration changes, or disclosing PHI.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Tricking clinicians/patients.

threats.name: Missing authentication
threats.description:
The product does not perform any authentication for functionality that requires a provable user identity or consumes a significant amount of resources.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Open endpoints exposed.

threats.name: Non-Compliance
threats.description:
The system deviates from security and data management best practices, standards, and legislation. Focus is on the organizational and operational management context in which a system or service is embedded. Non-compliance main threat characteristics are: The unlawfulness of personal data processing Lacking data lifecycle management: this relates to data minimization, storage limitation, and data subject control principles A lack of proper cybersecurity risk management

Attacker goal / impact: Legal: Violating HIPAA/GDPR/MDR requirements.

threats.name: Physical theft or loss of portable devices (PHI exposure)
threats.description: Portable medical devices—such as tablets, diagnostic readers, or home-use monitors—may store protected health information (PHI) locally. If such a device is lost or stolen without full-disk encryption or remote wipe capability, an unauthorized individual could access patient data, calibration settings, or device credentials.

threats.name: Repudiation
threats.description:
Repudiation is the rejection or denial of a performed action.

Attacker goal / impact: Audit: User denies performing an action.

threats.name: Reverse Engineering
threats.description:
Attackers decompile or reverse-engineer the mobile app to understand its functionality, extract sensitive data, or discover vulnerabilities.

Attacker goal / impact: IP Theft: Analyze code to find API keys/logic.

threats.name: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
threats.description:
An attacker could leverage insufficient logging and monitoring to carry out attacks without being detected, hindering security incident identification and response.

Attacker goal / impact: Response: Slow reaction to active breach.

threats.name: Security Misconfiguration (API)
threats.description:
Attackers might exploit unpatched flaws, services with insecure default configurations, or unprotected files and directories, potentially leading to unauthorized access or system compromise.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Unpatched flaws or open cloud buckets.

threats.name: Security Misconfiguration (Web and Mobile)
threats.description:
An attacker could exploit security misconfigurations to gain unauthorized access or functionality. This could include unpatched flaws, unprotected files, and directories, or default accounts.

Attacker goal / impact: Access: Default accounts/unprotected files.

threats.name: Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
threats.description:
Attackers could exploit SSRF vulnerabilities in APIs to cause internal services enumeration, information disclosure, bypassing firewalls, or server misuse.

Attacker goal / impact: Network Intrusion: API attacks internal cloud services.

threats.name: Session Hijacking
threats.description:
An attacker discovers/compromises the session management strategy and gains access to an object by impersonating another user or a service.

Attacker goal / impact: Account Takeover: Stolen session cookies.

threats.name: Side-channel data leakage
threats.description:
Sensitive data can be inadvertently exposed through logs, screenshots, or background apps.

Attacker goal / impact: Leakage: Screenshots or logs leak info to OS.

threats.name: Spoofing
threats.description:
Spoofing is where an attacker masquerades as a trusted entity to gain unauthorized access or deceive recipients.

Attacker goal / impact: Impersonation: Faking device or user identity.

threats.name: Tampering
threats.description:
Tampering with data involves unauthorized changes to digital information, often with harmful intent, making it unreliable and leading to serious consequences.

Attacker goal / impact: Integrity: Modifying data in transit/at rest.

threats.name: Tampering or firmware extraction
threats.description:
An attacker with physical, local, or privileged logical access extracts or tampers with the device’s firmware (via JTAG, UART, USB, removable storage, or an unauthenticated update channel), enabling reverse-engineering, creation of modified firmware images, or injection of malicious code that alters device behavior, exposes PHI, or creates persistent backdoors.

Attacker goal / impact: IP Theft: Extract firmware via JTAG/UART.

threats.name: Tampering with calibration data or safety thresholds
threats.description:
An attacker or unauthorized user modifies the device’s calibration constants, sensor offsets, or safety thresholds (e.g., pressure limits, temperature bounds, dosage cutoffs), causing inaccurate readings, unsafe therapy delivery, or disabled safety mechanisms.

Attacker goal / impact: Patient Safety: Disable safety limits or alter sensor readings.

threats.name: Time synchronization manipulation (affecting logs, alarms, safety timing)
threats.description: An attacker tampers with the device’s time source (NTP, GPS, internal RTC, or companion app clock) or manipulates time-stamping mechanisms, causing false timestamps for logs/telemetry, delayed or premature alarms and therapy actions, and incorrect sequencing of safety checks.

threats.name: Trojaned or attacker controlled app
threats.description:
Attacker violates the app store or update channel, loading an attacker controlled software version onto the Patient's cell phone.

Attacker goal / impact: Phishing: Fake app mimics the real medical app.

threats.name: Unauthorized parameter modification (e.g., dose rate, voltage, pacing interval)
threats.description: An attacker or unauthorized user modifies therapy or diagnostic parameters—such as infusion dose rate, stimulation voltage, pacing interval, or calibration settings—without proper authentication or authorization, potentially causing harm to patients or degrading device performance.

threats.name: Unawareness and Unintervenability
threats.description:
Insufficiently informing, involving or empowering individuals in the processing of personal data. This relates to: Lack of transparency: data subjects are unaware of the collection and/or processing of their data or the personal data of others. Lack of feedback: data subjects are insufficiently informed about the privacy impact they may cause to others using the system. Lack of intervenability: data subjects cannot access or manage their data.

Attacker goal / impact: Rights Violation: User cannot opt-out or see data.

threats.name: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
threats.description:
Attackers could exploit sensitive business flows in APIs, causing harm such as preventing legitimate users from purchasing a product or leading to inflation in a game's internal economy.

Attacker goal / impact: Abuse: Automation of business logic (e.g., spam).

threats.name: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
threats.description:
Attackers could exploit unrestricted resource consumption, leading to DoS due to resource starvation or increased operational costs.

Attacker goal / impact: DoS: API exhaustion/crash.

threats.name: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
threats.description:
Attackers might identify and compromise other APIs/services integrated with the target API, leading to sensitive information exposure, injections, or denial of service.

Attacker goal / impact: Supply Chain: Integrated 3rd party API is compromised.

threats.name: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
threats.description:
An attacker could target vulnerable and outdated components, such as libraries, frameworks, and other software modules, to execute various attacks.

Attacker goal / impact: Exploit: Using libraries with CVEs (e.g., Log4j).

threats.name: Weak Server-Side Controls
threats.description:
Servers interacting with the mobile app may have vulnerabilities due to improper authentication, authorization, or input validation.

Attacker goal / impact: Bypass: Trusting client input without validation.

mitigations.name: Server-Side Command Validation and Device/Session Binding
mitigations.description: Enforce server-side validation of every sensitive request—including device identity, user session, app signature, and allowed operation scopes—so proxied or replayed commands from a rogue local app cannot modify therapy parameters, access PHI, or impersonate the legitimate medical app.

mitigations.name: Strict App-to-App Isolation With Authenticated IPC and Scoped Permissions
mitigations.description: Require all inter-app communication (deep links, intents, URL schemes, IPC channels) to use authenticated, signed, or token-bound requests, and ensure the medical app accepts commands only from verified, whitelisted sources, preventing untrusted apps on the same phone from proxying or relaying malicious actions.

mitigations.name: Deny Access by Default
mitigations.description: Enforce a deny-by-default access control policy, where no user, system, or plugin is granted access unless explicitly allowed by defined rules. Default behavior should reject all requests until specific permissions are granted through access policies or allow-lists.
mitigations.consideration: Define explicit allow-lists for all actions, users, services, and data access. - Configure default access controls to deny any request unless explicitly authorized. - ensure all new plugins, APIs, and user roles are evaluated for access restrictions before deployment. - Review access control configurations regularly to ensure no implicit permissions exist. - Enforce access policies through infrastructure-as-code or configuration Management to prevent misconfigurations.
mitigations.explanation: Deny-by-default policies ensure that access is never assumed or open by default. Instead, each access request must meet pre-approved conditions before being granted. This limits the potential attack surface and prevents unauthorized interactions. By configuring allow-lists and enforcing explicit permissions at every layer—from API gateways to internal services, organizations prevent unintended access. Regular audits help detect and remove outdated or overly permissive rules.
mitigations.example: - AWS IAM: IAM policies can be configured to deny all access unless specifically allowed via policies. - Google Cloud IAM uses allow-based roles where no access is granted until explicitly permitted. - API Gateways: Only routes explicitly defined in the gateway are reachable; others are denied by default. - Azure Resource Manager enforces deny-by-default behavior in RBAC assignments. - Kubernetes Network Policies deny all pod-to-pod communication by default unless allow-rules are defined.

mitigations.name: Develop a comprehensive threat model
mitigations.description: Identify and evaluate potential threats to systems by analyzing assets, attack surfaces, and vulnerabilities. Develop a structured threat model to understand how attackers could exploit weaknesses and to prioritize risks. Use this model to inform future security design and decision-making.
mitigations.consideration: Identify assets, users, and data flows - Map attack surfaces and trust boundaries - Enumerate threats using frameworks like STRIDE or MITRE ATT&CK - assess likelihood and impact for risk prioritization - Involve cross-functional teams (Security, dev, ops) - update the model regularly to reflect system changes
mitigations.explanation: Threat modeling involves identifying system assets, mapping how data flows between components, and evaluating how attackers might exploit vulnerabilities. Teams use frameworks like STRIDE to classify threats and assess risks. The model guides secure design and helps prioritize mitigations based on potential impact.
mitigations.example: Devici for structured threat modeling and risk analysis - SD Elements (SDE) for integrating threat modeling into secure development workflows - MITRE ATT&CK for identifying and mapping adversary techniques - Draw.io or Lucidchart for visualizing system architecture and data flow

mitigations.name: Enforce record ownership in models
mitigations.description: Implement strict ownership checks in your data models to ensure users can only access their own records. Validate user permissions at the model level to prevent unauthorized access to functionality and data.
mitigations.consideration: Apply ownership checks at all access layers, including APIs, services, and UI. - Use unique user identifiers to associate records with owners. - Employ RBAC to Define and Enforce access boundaries based on ownership. - Log access attempts and Monitor for violations or anomalies. - regularly Review access rules to reflect changes in user roles or system structure. - Provide secure coding guidelines to help developers implement consistent ownership checks.
mitigations.explanation: Record ownership enforcement involves linking each data entry to a specific user and validating ownership before granting access. This check should be implemented at the model or middleware level to ensure it applies regardless of how data is accessed. Role-based access controls (RBAC) can refine permissions to only allow users to interact with their own records. Ownership checks must be applied consistently across all components, with logging and alerting to detect unauthorized access attempts.
mitigations.example: - AWS IAM: Enables permissions based on ownership of specific resources. - OAuth 2.0: Scopes access tokens to user-specific data, enforcing ownership. - Django: Uses mixins and decorators to restrict views to owner’s records. - Microsoft Azure AD: Supports RBAC to enforce access rules at resource levels. - Spring Security: Supports annotations for method-level ownership checks in Java apps.

mitigations.name: Implement Access Control Measures
mitigations.description: Implement robust access control mechanisms to validate and authorize each entity's actions within the system. Ensure that permissions are strictly enforced to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data and functionality. Regularly review and update access controls to address vulnerabilities and adhere to the principle of least privilege.
mitigations.consideration: Define clear access policies based on job responsibilities and data sensitivity - Use least privilege as a default for all roles and permissions - Separate duties across roles to reduce risk from over-privileged accounts - Review and update access rights regularly, especially after role changes - Apply fine-grained access control at the resource, function, and data level
mitigations.explanation: Access control ensures users and systems only access what they need based on roles and responsibilities. By applying least privilege and separating duties, organizations reduce the risk of abuse or error. Fine-grained controls restrict access to specific data or functions, and regular reviews ensure permissions stay aligned with evolving roles.
mitigations.example: AWS IAM / Azure RBAC: Define and manage granular role-based access - Okta / Keycloak: Centralize user role Management and access policies - OPA (Open Policy Agent): Enforce fine-grained access at the application level - GitLab / GitHub roles: control project and repository access by role - GCP IAM Conditions: Apply attribute-based access rules for resources

mitigations.name: Implement access control mechanisms
mitigations.description: Implement access control mechanisms consistently across the application to ensure that every user action is explicitly authorized. Validate permissions at all entry points, including API endpoints, services, and internal functions, to prevent unauthorized access to data and functionality.
mitigations.consideration: - Define and document a unified access control strategy for all system components. - Enforce access control at multiple layers (API gateway, backend services, databases). - Use centralized policy engines (e.g., RBAC or ABAC) to apply consistent rules. - Perform static and dynamic testing to identify endpoints lacking access checks. - Monitor access patterns and log unauthorized attempts for analysis. - Train developers to apply consistent authorization checks during development.
mitigations.explanation: Consistent access control ensures that no part of the application allows unauthorized access due to missing or inconsistent permission checks. Implementing centralized enforcement mechanisms like RBAC or ABAC ensures rules are uniformly applied across all endpoints and services. Security tools should verify that access control policies are in place at every interaction point. Logging, audits, and testing tools help maintain coverage and identify violations over time.
mitigations.example: - AWS IAM for managing user permissions and roles. - OAuth 2.0 for delegated access control in APIs, ensuring users can only access resources they are authorized to. - API Gateway services (e.g., Amazon API Gateway, Azure API Management) that enforce access policies at the function level. - Open Policy Agent (OPA) for implementing fine-grained access control based on policies. - Role-based access control features in platforms like Microsoft Azure Active Directory.

mitigations.name: Implement Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
mitigations.description: Implement Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) to enforce access decisions based on user attributes like role, location, and resource characteristics. Ensure that access is granted only to authorized users, preventing lateral movement, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to functions or data.
mitigations.consideration: ensure attributes used for access control are accurate and up-to-date to prevent unauthorized access. - implement logging and monitoring of access requests to detect and respond to anomalies. - regularly Audit access policies to Identify and rectify potential gaps or misconfigurations. - Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to strengthen access control. - Educate users on the importance of attribute accuracy and the risks of privilege escalation.
mitigations.explanation: ABAC implementation involves defining user attributes, resource characteristics, and environmental conditions to create access policies. These policies evaluate attributes dynamically at the time of access requests, ensuring that only users meeting specific criteria can access resources. The system utilizes a policy engine to process requests, applying rules that reflect the least privilege principle. Regular audits and real-time monitoring ensure the detection of unauthorized access attempts.
mitigations.example: Examples of technology that implement Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) include - AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Azure Active Directory Conditional Access - Okta Identity Cloud - Google Cloud IAM. - Solutions like Axiomatics Policy Server and Auth0 provide ABAC capabilities. These technologies allow for dynamic access control based on user attributes and contextual information.

mitigations.name: Deploy anti-brute force protections
mitigations.description: Implement anti-brute force protections at all authentication endpoints to prevent unauthorized access. This includes account lockout policies, rate limiting, and CAPTCHA challenges after a specified number of failed login attempts.
mitigations.consideration: implement account lockout policies to temporarily Disable accounts after failed login attempts - Apply rate limiting to Restrict repeated login attempts from the same source within a short timeframe - Use CAPTCHA challenges after multiple failed attempts to block automated attacks - implement IP blacklisting for persistent attackers - Monitor and Log login attempts for suspicious patterns - test the effectiveness of protections through simulated attacks
mitigations.explanation: To defend against brute-force attacks, authentication endpoints must enforce layered protections. Account lockout policies temporarily disable access after repeated failures, while rate limiting restricts login attempts in a short timeframe. CAPTCHA challenges stop automated tools, and IP blacklisting blocks persistent attackers. Logging and regular testing ensure these controls remain effective against evolving threats.
mitigations.example: Cloudflare Bot Management: Enforces rate limiting and CAPTCHA after failed attempts - Google reCAPTCHA: Blocks automated login attempts using challenge-response - AWS WAF: Supports IP-based login throttling and blocking rules - Fail2Ban: Analyzes logs and blacklists IPs after repeated failures - Okta: Implements lockout policies and multi-Layer login defenses - Microsoft Azure AD: Provides account lockout, CAPTCHA, and adaptive risk-based controls

mitigations.name: Implement strong authentication with 2FA or MFA.
mitigations.description: Implement Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) or Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) to enhance identity verification for all users.
mitigations.consideration: - Select authentication methods that combine at least two distinct factors (e.g., password + TOTP or hardware token) - Require biometric factors where possible for enhanced security. - Support widely adopted authenticators like TOTP apps or FIDO2 devices - Enforce MFA for all users, especially for privileged accounts - Ensure fallback mechanisms are secure and limited
mitigations.explanation: Strong authentication with 2FA or MFA uses two or more factors—like passwords and TOTP apps or hardware tokens—to verify user identity. Even if a password is compromised, a second factor helps prevent unauthorized access. MFA should be enforced across all login flows, including admin panels and APIs, to reduce the risk of account takeover and credential-based attacks.
mitigations.example: - Google / Microsoft Authenticator: TOTP apps for 2FA - YubiKey / SoloKey: Hardware tokens using FIDO2/U2F - Duo Security: Enterprise MFA with multiple factor types - GitHub / AWS / Salesforce: Offer built-in MFA enforcement - Authy: Cross-device TOTP support with cloud sync

mitigations.name: Map all authentication flows
mitigations.description: Identify and document all authentication flows across the system, including APIs, web, and mobile entry points. Include methods used (e.g., OAuth, SAML), token generation and expiration practices, and secure password storage. Regularly review and update this documentation to mitigate risks from broken or outdated authentication mechanisms.
mitigations.consideration: Identify all entry points where authentication occurs, including APIs, Web apps, and mobile platforms. - document the methods used for authentication and how credentials or tokens are validated. - Include token expiration policies, refresh flows, and storage mechanisms. - verify password storage practices Use secure hashing algorithms. - update the documentation regularly to reflect system changes or new access points. - Involve relevant teams to Validate completeness and accuracy
mitigations.explanation: Mapping authentication flows is essential to identify hidden entry points that could be exploited by attackers. Without a full inventory, it's easy to overlook outdated, duplicated, or misconfigured flows that increase the risk of credential misuse or session hijacking. A clear map improves visibility, simplifies risk analysis, and supports more effective access control and incident response planning.
mitigations.example: Use Postman + Auth logs (e.g., CloudTrail, SIEM) to manually trace Real authentication journeys. - Use IAM platforms to visualize configured flows. - Use Burp/ZAP to catch any hidden or forgotten endpoints during red teaming.

mitigations.name: Secure credential recovery endpoints
mitigations.description: Implement strong security measures for credential recovery endpoints, including rate limiting, CAPTCHA, and multi-factor authentication. Ensure that recovery processes verify user identity rigorously and log all recovery attempts for monitoring and auditing.
mitigations.consideration: ensure recovery links expire after a short duration to prevent misuse. - implement email or SMS verification for any changes to recovery information. - Use unique, unpredictable tokens for recovery processes to prevent enumeration attacks. - regularly Review and update recovery procedures to address emerging threats. - Educate users on recognizing phishing attempts related to recovery processes.
mitigations.explanation: Credential recovery endpoints must enforce secure practices to prevent abuse. Recovery links should expire quickly to reduce the risk of reuse. Each recovery attempt should generate a unique, unpredictable token to prevent guessing or enumeration. Any change to recovery information should trigger email or SMS-based verification. Regular reviews ensure recovery workflows stay updated, while user training helps prevent phishing and social engineering attacks.
mitigations.example: Google account recovery: uses MFA and token-based verification with expiration - Authy: Sends SMS codes for recovery verification - LastPass: Implements CAPTCHA, rate limiting, and email verification for changes - Okta: Provides secure, customizable identity recovery workflows - Microsoft Azure AD: Offers Advanced recovery protections, including token expiration - Duo Security: Supports multi-factor recovery verification with Audit logging

mitigations.name: Implement random and unpredictable record IDs
mitigations.description: Use random and unpredictable values, such as GUIDs, for record IDs to prevent unauthorized access.
mitigations.consideration: Use cryptographically secure random number generators to create record IDs (e.g., uuid V4) - Avoid sequential or incremental IDs, which can be guessed or enumerated by attackers - ensure IDs are long enough to prevent brute-force Discovery - implement server-side ID generation to reduce exposure from client-controlled input - Review and test ID generation mechanisms regularly to ensure randomness and resistance to prediction attacks
mitigations.explanation: Predictable record IDs (like auto-incrementing numbers) can expose APIs to enumeration and unauthorized access. To prevent this, IDs should be generated using cryptographically secure random number generators, such as UUID v4. These IDs should be long, unique, and generated server-side to prevent tampering or guessing. Regular reviews and tests of the ID generation process ensure continued resistance to prediction-based attacks.
mitigations.example: uuid V4 libraries: generate secure, random identifiers using cryptographic RNGs - Node.js uuid Package: Commonly used to generate unpredictable record IDs - Firebase Firestore: Automatically Assigns non-sequential document IDs - AWS DynamoDB: Supports random partition keys to Avoid predictable patterns - OWASP ZAP: can be used to test for ID predictability or enumeration vulnerabilities - Python secrets module: generates secure random strings for record IDs

mitigations.name: Implement record-level authorization checks for all API endpoints
mitigations.description: Enforce record-level authorization checks for all API endpoints. Validate that the logged-in user has the necessary permissions for each record accessed based on client input in every relevant function.
mitigations.consideration: ensure robust authentication mechanisms are in place to verify user identity before authorization checks. - Enforce record-level authorization in every API method accessing data - Use role- or attribute-based access control to simplify permission logic - conduct Security testing to Validate that authorization logic cannot be bypassed
mitigations.explanation: Record-level authorization ensures users access only data they are permitted to see. API methods must include explicit checks verifying the user’s identity and permissions for each record accessed. Role- or attribute-based access control can help manage these permissions efficiently. Security testing, including authorization bypass tests, is essential to verify that unauthorized users cannot access or manipulate protected data.
mitigations.example: - OAuth 2.0: Supports fine-grained scopes for user-specific API access - AWS IAM: Applies user roles to restrict access to specific resources - Firebase Security Rules: Enforces user- and attribute-based access at the data level - Spring Security: Supports method- and object-level authorization logic - Auth0: Implements RBAC and ABAC for record-based access decisions - Casbin: A lightweight policy engine supporting per-record access enforcement

mitigations.name: Implement property-level access controls
mitigations.description: Implement access controls to restrict users from viewing or modifying object properties based on their authorization level.
mitigations.consideration: limit user access to Only the properties of objects they are authorized to view or modify - Use a centralized access control mechanism to Enforce property-level rules consistently - regularly Audit access control logic to Identify misconfigurations or excessive privileges - Log access to sensitive properties for traceability and incident response - Train developers on secure handling of user permissions at the property level
mitigations.explanation: Property-level access controls ensure users can only view or modify specific object properties they are authorized to access. This is enforced through centralized authorization logic that checks user roles, attributes, or policies before granting access. Each sensitive property should have associated access rules. Logs of access attempts and regular audits help identify misconfigurations or over-permissive access. Developer training ensures secure implementation.
mitigations.example: - OAuth 2.0 scopes: Restrict access to specific user data fields - AWS IAM Policies: Allow fine-grained access to object attributes - RBAC in databases: Controls column-level access per role - JWT claims: Carry property-level access rules for APIs - ABAC: Enforces access using user and resource attributes - Spring Security: Supports field-level restrictions in Java apps

mitigations.name: Implement schema-based response validation
mitigations.description: Enforce schema-based response validation for all API methods to ensure only authorized object properties are returned, preventing unauthorized access to sensitive data.
mitigations.consideration: Define strict response schemas for each API to limit exposed fields - Validate responses before sending them to users using Schema rules - update schemas regularly to reflect changes in data sensitivity or access rules - Enforce Schema-level validation errors to prevent fallback to full object exposure - handle errors securely to Avoid leaking sensitive info - Monitor response validation failures and investigate anomalies
mitigations.explanation: Schema-based response validation ensures only approved fields are returned by the API. JSON or XML schemas define allowed properties for each endpoint and user context. Responses are validated before being sent to the client, blocking unintended data exposure. Validation failures must be logged and investigated. Error messages should be generic to prevent information leakage. Schema reviews ensure alignment with security and data classification policies.
mitigations.example: GraphQL schemas: Restrict returned fields based on roles and queries - Ajv / Joi: JavaScript libraries for validating JSON responses against schemas - AWS API gateway: Enforces Schema validation for rest APIs - OpenAPI / Swagger: Supports response Schema definitions and validation - Apigee: Provides Schema enforcement and response inspection features - Zally: Enforces Schema rules in OpenAPI contracts during CI/CD

mitigations.name: Limit property exposure
mitigations.description: Limit property exposure by implementing fine-grained access controls. Ensure that only authorized users can access sensitive object properties. Replace automatic object serialization or default field exposure with explicit selection of properties to include in API responses, views, or outputs. This reduces the risk of unintentionally leaking sensitive data.
mitigations.consideration: - Avoid exposing object properties by default; expose only what's necessary - Replace generic serialization with explicitly defined fields for output - Remove sensitive or unused properties from API responses and UI layers - Use data transformation layers (e.g., DTOs or serializers) to control exposure - Review property exposure across endpoints and adjust based on role and context - Train developers to recognize overexposure risks in APIs and object mappings
mitigations.explanation: Limiting property exposure means explicitly defining which object fields are returned to users instead of relying on default serialization. Automatically exposing entire objects can leak sensitive data. Use DTOs, serializers, or view models to control what properties are included. Tailor responses to the user's role or context, and audit API outputs to catch overexposed fields. This reduces the risk of data leakage and supports the principle of least privilege.
mitigations.example: Spring Boot DTOs: expose Only selected fields in API responses - Django rest framework serializers: control which fields appear in responses - GraphQL resolvers: Return Only authorized fields per query context - TypeScript interfaces or class transformers: Shape exposed objects explicitly - Express.js with manual res.json(): Select which fields to Include in outputs - Postman or Burp Suite: used to Audit and detect overexposed fields

mitigations.name: Implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
mitigations.description: Restrict system access by assigning permissions based on user or service roles. RBAC ensures that users, applications, or LLMs can only access resources necessary for their role, minimizing the risk of unauthorized actions. Define roles with clear scopes, assign them to entities based on operational needs.
mitigations.consideration: Identify all user and Service roles based on operational needs. - Define permissions clearly for each role and follow the principle of least privilege when assigning permissions. - implement a robust onboarding and offboarding process to manage role assignments. - Monitor access patterns to detect misuse or privilege escalation. - regularly Review and update roles to reflect changes in responsibilities or system architecture.
mitigations.explanation: RBAC implementation involves defining distinct user roles with specific permissions aligned to job functions. Access control decisions are made based on these roles, ensuring users only access resources necessary for their duties. Authorization checks are enforced at all entry points, validating user roles against requested actions. Regular audits and monitoring track role assignments, while automated tools assist in detecting anomalies and ensuring compliance with least privilege principles.
mitigations.example: Examples of technology that implement RBAC include: - Microsoft Azure Active Directory - AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Okta, and Google Cloud Identity. - Tools like HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes RBAC can enforce role-based permissions. - Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) solutions, such as Splunk and IBM QRadar, can monitor and audit role assignments and access patterns to ensure compliance with least privilege principles.

mitigations.name: Validate User Input
mitigations.description: Implement strict input validation to ensure user-provided data adheres to expected formats, types, and constraints. Reject or sanitize any input that does not meet these criteria to prevent potential security vulnerabilities such as injection attacks or unauthorized access.
mitigations.consideration: Use whitelisting for acceptable input formats and values. - implement regular expressions to Enforce input patterns. - limit input length to mitigate buffer overflow risks. - Validate data types explicitly - Employ context-aware encoding for output. -Add rate limiting to block brute-force input - Use Security libraries or frameworks with built-in validation. - Log and Monitor invalid input for analysis.
mitigations.explanation: Input validation ensures user data is clean, expected, and secure before processing. Strong validation prevents injection, overflow, and brute-force attacks. Input rules should align with business logic, and validation must happen both client- and server-side. Monitoring rejected inputs can help identify attack patterns and improve defenses over time.
mitigations.example: - Joi (Node.js): Define and enforce input schemas using clear syntax - Validator.js: Validate and sanitize strings (e.g., emails, URLs) - Express-validator: Middleware for input validation in Express apps - Yup (JavaScript/TypeScript): Schema validation for form inputs - OWASP ESAPI: Java library for input validation and encoding

mitigations.name: Implement Parameterization
mitigations.description: Use parameterized queries and prepared statements to enforce strict separation of code and data in database and OS operations, preventing injection attacks. Ensure input values are bound to placeholders rather than concatenated into code strings.
mitigations.consideration: Enforce Use of parameterized APIs or libraries for all command and database operations. - Audit codebases to Identify and eliminate unsafe string concatenation. - Validate all input values before binding them to parameters. - ensure consistent Use of prepared statements in both backend and frontend frameworks. - regularly test parameter handling through code reviews and Security audits.
mitigations.explanation: Parameterization works by clearly separating user input from the command or query structure. Instead of injecting input directly into commands, parameters are used as placeholders, which prevents injection attacks. This technique ensures inputs are interpreted strictly as data, not executable code. Regular audits and validations help maintain its effectiveness, especially in preventing OS and database-level injection threats.
mitigations.example: - For OS Command Injection, libraries like Apache Commons Exec and Python's subprocess module provide methods to safely execute commands with parameters. - In Python, use the subprocess.run(["cmd", param]) pattern. - In Java, use PreparedStatement to bind variables in SQL queries. - In web apps, frameworks like React escape inputs in templates, and libraries like DOMPurify sanitize HTML. - Use ORMs like SQLAlchemy or Entity Framework to enforce parameterization automatically.

mitigations.name: Implement a secure secret management solution
mitigations.description: Store all credentials in a secure, encrypted secret management solution, ensuring they are not hard-coded in the application. Restrict access to these secrets to authorized components only, and regularly audit for potential credential leakage in logs and code.
mitigations.consideration: Choose a secret Management solution that Fits your architecture and operational needs - Apply environment-specific configurations to isolate secrets by stage - ensure secrets are rotated regularly using automated processes - Monitor and Audit secret access for unusual activity - Educate developers on secure handling of secrets and available tooling
mitigations.explanation: A secure secret management solution stores sensitive credentials in an encrypted vault. Applications access these secrets through secure APIs, avoiding exposure in code or config files. Permissions control access, while logging and audits track usage. Regular rotation and monitoring help reduce the risk of leaks and ensure secrets remain up to date.
mitigations.example: HashiCorp Vault: centralized tool for encrypted secret storage - AWS secrets Manager: manages and rotates secrets in AWS - Azure Key Vault: stores and secures secrets, keys, and certs - CyberArk Conjur: Open-source tool for app and user secret access - Google secret Manager: Google’s Vault for keys, certs, and tokens

mitigations.name: Classify data sensitivity
mitigations.description: Classify data based on its sensitivity level (such as public, internal, confidential, or restricted) and apply appropriate controls for each category. This ensures that sensitive information is handled securely, meets compliance requirements, and is protected from unauthorized access or disclosure.
mitigations.consideration: Define clear classification tiers based on regulatory, legal, and business risk factors. - Train personnel to recognize and handle each classification level correctly. - Use automated tools to detect, label, and tag sensitive data across systems. - Enforce different access control policies and encryption requirements per data class. - Review and update classification schemes regularly based on evolving risks. - Monitor access to sensitive data and generate alerts on anomalous activity.
mitigations.explanation: Data classification involves identifying and labeling information based on its sensitivity and risk level. This process enables organizations to apply the correct security controls to different types of data, such as encryption, access restrictions, and audit logging. Automated classification tools streamline enforcement by tagging sensitive information in real time. Ongoing monitoring and access reviews help detect misuse and support compliance obligations.
mitigations.example: Symantec DLP for automatic classification and protection - Microsoft Information protection for tagging and access control - AWS Macie for discovering and labeling sensitive data in cloud storage - VeraCrypt for encrypting sensitive files - HashiCorp Vault for classified data Key Management - IBM Guardium for monitoring access to protected data

mitigations.name: Encrypt all data in transit using secure protocols.
mitigations.description: Encrypt all data in transit using current, secure communication protocols such as TLS 1.3. Ensure all services and APIs are authenticated and data is encrypted between endpoints to protect against interception and tampering. Validate implementation against cryptographic best practices, and avoid deprecated or insecure protocols. Regularly review and update configurations to maintain data integrity and confidentiality.
mitigations.consideration: - Use strong, modern encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.3) and secure cipher suites. - Implement certificate pinning to protect against man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks. - Ensure third-party libraries and dependencies related to cryptography are kept up to date. - Conduct regular audits and penetration tests to verify secure implementation of encryption in transit. - Use mutual TLS (mTLS) where appropriate to authenticate both client and server.
mitigations.explanation: Securing data in transit involves encrypting all communications between clients, servers, and third-party systems using modern protocols like TLS 1.3. Certificate pinning strengthens MITM defenses, while mutual TLS ensures both endpoints are authenticated. Keeping libraries updated prevents the use of known-vulnerable cryptographic methods. Regular testing and validation confirm correct implementation and allow prompt remediation of weaknesses in encrypted communication paths.
mitigations.example: - TLS 1.3 for end-to-end encrypted communication - HTTPS for secure web traffic - Mutual TLS (mTLS) for API authentication - Certificate pinning in mobile apps - OpenSSL for implementing strong cryptographic protocols - Cloudflare WAF to inspect and secure encrypted traffic - VPNs for encrypted connections to external systems

mitigations.name: Encrypt all sensitive data in transit and at rest
mitigations.description: Encrypt all sensitive data both in transit and at rest to protect it from unauthorized access. Implement strong encryption protocols for data flows crossing trust boundaries and ensure that sensitive information is stored securely using encryption methods that meet industry standards.
mitigations.consideration: - Use strong encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2+, AES-256) and avoid weak or outdated algorithms - Encrypt data stored on disks, databases, and backups - Apply encryption to data in transit across internal and external networks - Ensure encryption is enabled by default in systems handling sensitive data - Ensure encryption keys are securely managed and rotated regularly
mitigations.explanation: Sensitive data should be encrypted both at rest and in transit using strong protocols like AES-256 and TLS 1.2+. Encryption must be applied to all data crossing trust boundaries, such as between services or across networks. Keys should be stored securely and rotated regularly. Avoid weak algorithms and ensure encryption settings follow industry best practices by default.
mitigations.example: AES (Advanced encryption Standard) for encrypting data at rest - TLS (Transport Layer Security) for securing data in transit - AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for secure Key Management - Microsoft Azure Disk encryption for encrypting virtual machine disks - VeraCrypt for creating encrypted containers for sensitive files - BitLocker for encrypting entire drives on Windows devices

mitigations.name: Implement up-to-date encryption standards
mitigations.description: Apply the latest industry-approved encryption standards to protect sensitive data. Ensure cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and key management practices are regularly updated to mitigate emerging threats and comply with evolving security requirements.
mitigations.consideration: - Periodically assess encryption configurations to ensure compliance with current standards (e.g., NIST, ISO). - Replace outdated algorithms (e.g., SHA-1, RSA-1024) with modern, secure alternatives (e.g., AES-256, SHA-3, ECC). - Enforce key rotation schedules and ensure use of strong, unique keys. - Monitor regulatory and vendor guidance for updates to approved encryption protocols. - Train developers on proper use of cryptographic libraries and deprecation timelines.
mitigations.explanation: Keeping encryption mechanisms up to date requires continuous monitoring of cryptographic standards and replacing deprecated algorithms. This includes migrating from older protocols like TLS 1.1 to secure versions like TLS 1.3, using secure key lengths, and leveraging services that automatically adopt current best practices. Up-to-date encryption strengthens resilience against known exploits and ensures compliance with regulatory frameworks such as GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS.
mitigations.example: - AWS KMS: Supports AES-256 and automatic key rotation. - Azure Key Vault: Uses FIPS 140-2 validated modules. - Google Cloud Encryption: Enforces TLS 1.3, supports customer-managed keys. - OpenSSL 3.x: Includes modern cipher suites. - Cloudflare: Uses TLS 1.3 for secure web traffic. - Apple CryptoKit: Offers current encryption APIs for iOS/macOS.

mitigations.name: Implement an anonymity system
mitigations.description: Implement an anonymity system that obscures users' identities and personal data during digital interactions. Ensure that no identifiable information, such as location or user actions, is exposed. Utilize tools and methods that prevent linking, identifying, and detecting threats, thereby minimizing data disclosure risks.
mitigations.consideration: - Avoid collecting PII such as IP addresses and location data - Replace persistent identifiers with rotating session tokens - Use mix networks, onion routing, or VPNs to obscure source IPs - Apply data minimization principles, only collect what's strictly necessary - Remove or obfuscate metadata from transmitted content - Conduct regular privacy audits to identify and mitigate potential tracking vectors - Educate users and developers about fingerprinting risks and how to reduce traceability
mitigations.explanation: The anonymity system hides user identities by avoiding persistent identifiers, masking network-level metadata, and rotating session data. It limits data collection, uses encryption, and avoids storing identifiable information. These measures prevent profiling and tracking during digital interactions.
mitigations.example: Tor: Enables anonymous Web access. - signal: Encrypts messages and hides metadata. - VPNs: mask IP and location data. - ARX: Anonymizes structured datasets. - Tails OS: Preserves anonymity by design.

mitigations.name: Implement privacy-preserving authentication methods.
mitigations.description: Implement privacy-preserving authentication methods that verify user or device identities while minimizing personal information disclosure. Use techniques that ensure secure and reliable authentication without compromising user privacy. Focus on reducing the amount of sensitive data collected and shared during the authentication process.
mitigations.consideration: Utilize zero-knowledge proofs to authenticate users without revealing sensitive Information - implement multi-factor authentication that relies on less intrusive data sources - Use temporary or Session-based identifiers instead of persistent identifiers - regularly Audit authentication logs to minimize data retention and exposure - ensure that authentication systems are Designed to limit data sharing to necessary parties Only, Avoid centralized storage of authentication data where possible
mitigations.explanation: Key characteristics of privacy-preserving authentication include limiting data disclosure, supporting anonymous or pseudonymous access, using secure encryption, and decentralization. Techniques like zero-knowledge proofs allow validation without revealing sensitive information. These methods reduce privacy risks in sensitive contexts such as banking or digital identity verification.
mitigations.example: - ZK-SNARKs (Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge) for blockchain transactions. - FIDO2/WebAuthn for passwordless authentication. - Privacy-focused identity providers like uPort or Sovrin. - Temporary session tokens in OAuth 2.0. - Decentralized authentication tools that do not require user registration with a central server.

mitigations.name: Implement privacy-preserving cryptographic protocols
mitigations.description: Use privacy-preserving cryptographic protocols to secure communication and data processing while minimizing data exposure. Prioritize methods such as homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation (SMC), and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to protect sensitive data during operations. Regularly update protocols to address evolving threats.
mitigations.consideration: Use Homomorphic encryption to compute on encrypted data. - implement secure multi-party computation (SMC) to collaborate without exposing inputs. - Apply ZKPs for private verification. - Utilize Oblivious Transfer for anonymous data exchange. - incorporate differential privacy to protect query responses. - Use private set intersection for safe data comparison.
mitigations.explanation: Privacy-preserving cryptographic protocols allow data to remain confidential during processing and communication. Homomorphic encryption enables computation on encrypted data. SMC lets parties jointly compute without revealing inputs. ZKPs verify facts without exposing them. Oblivious transfer hides which data was shared. These methods support secure, private data workflows.
mitigations.example: Microsoft SEAL: Implements Homomorphic encryption for secure computation. - MP-SPDZ: a framework for secure multi-party computation. - Zokrates: ZKP toolkit for smart contracts on Ethereum. - Obliv-'C': Programming language for Oblivious Transfer and secure computation. - OpenDP: Implements differential privacy in statistical analysis. - PSI by Facebook/OpenMined: Enables private set intersection for contact discovery.

mitigations.name: Implement Private Information Retrieval (PIR) techniques.
mitigations.description: Implement PIR techniques that allow users to retrieve specific data from databases without revealing which items are accessed. Ensure the process protects query privacy, uses secure server models, and supports efficiency and scalability in sensitive systems.
mitigations.consideration: ensure PIR implementations Maintain query privacy under both single- and multi-server models. - Choose between computational or Information-theoretic PIR based on system constraints. - evaluate performance trade-offs, especially for large-scale databases. - Apply PIR in scenarios requiring query confidentiality, such as cloud or library access. - Monitor usage patterns and Log performance for optimization and anomaly detection.
mitigations.explanation: PIR techniques enable users to retrieve data without disclosing their query to the server. Systems may use computational PIR (based on mathematical hardness assumptions) or information-theoretic PIR (relying on multiple non-colluding servers). These techniques preserve privacy while balancing performance, with trade-offs in efficiency and scalability depending on the implementation.
mitigations.example: Oblivious Transfer protocols: used in systems that allow data Retrieval without query exposure. - multi-server PIR frameworks: like Sharemind and Enigma, where no single server knows the full query. - Homomorphic encryption-based PIR: Microsoft SEAL or IBM HELib allow computation on encrypted data. - cloud file Retrieval systems: Let users access specific files without revealing file interests.

mitigations.name: Implement pseudonymity systems
mitigations.description: Implement pseudonymity systems to enable users to perform activities under a pseudonym, safeguarding their real identities. Ensure that the system maintains accountability for actions taken under these pseudonyms while preventing direct identification. Regularly assess and minimize data collection, processing, and sharing to align with the principle of data minimization.
mitigations.consideration: Use distinct pseudonyms for different contexts to prevent cross-linking. - ensure pseudonym systems support traceability for accountability where legally required. - combine pseudonymity with PETs like encryption and anonymous communications. - Design with legal and ethical boundaries in mind to prevent misuse or profiling.
mitigations.explanation: Pseudonymity systems let users act without revealing real identities, supporting privacy and trusted interactions. By assigning distinct pseudonyms across contexts, they prevent linkability. When paired with PETs, they enhance confidentiality. Design must support accountability when needed and avoid misuse, profiling, or legal violations.
mitigations.example: Use UUIDs or hash functions to generate pseudonymous user IDs. - Integrate tools like SimpleLogin for pseudonymous email addresses. - Apply consistent pseudonyms using salted hashes across sessions. - combine with encryption libraries (e.g., libsodium) to prevent linkability. - Use Tor hidden services for pseudonymous Service hosting.

mitigations.name: Encrypted Local Storage With Hardware-Backed Key Protection
mitigations.description: Encrypt all sensitive data at rest—including PHI, logs, cached telemetry, and configuration files—using hardware-backed keys stored in a secure element or trusted execution environment, preventing attackers with physical or local access from reading or exporting stored data even if they extract raw memory or filesystem contents.

mitigations.name: Restricted Local Access Surfaces With Secure Interfaces and Continuous Monitoring
mitigations.description: Disable or tightly control local access pathways (USB, removable media, debug ports, local services), enforce authenticated and policy-validated access for any data retrieval, and monitor for anomalous read/export patterns, ensuring attackers cannot use exposed interfaces or service vulnerabilities to exfiltrate device data.

mitigations.name: Implement Distributed Architecture
mitigations.description: Deploy multiple instances of your application across different servers to ensure horizontal scaling and improve resilience against Denial of Service attacks.
mitigations.consideration: Utilize load balancers to distribute incoming traffic evenly across instances. - implement auto-scaling to dynamically adjust resources based on traffic spikes. - implement redundancy in server locations to prevent single points of failure. - Use caching mechanisms to reduce load on application servers. - Monitor traffic patterns to Identify and respond to potential DoS attempts quickly. - regularly test the architecture for vulnerabilities and performance under stress.
mitigations.explanation: Deploy services across multiple nodes and regions to eliminate single points of failure. Use load balancers to evenly distribute traffic and auto-scaling to adjust compute capacity dynamically. Integrate caching layers to optimize performance and monitor traffic patterns to detect and mitigate DoS attacks in real time. It should be complemented with a strong incident response program to ensure quick detection, investigation, and recovery from disruptions.
mitigations.example: Examples of technology that implement a distributed architecture include - Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic Load Balancing - Google Cloud Load Balancing - Microsoft Azure Load Balancer for traffic distribution. - Kubernetes can manage containerized applications across multiple nodes, while Cloudflare and Akamai provide content delivery networks (CDNs) that cache content and absorb traffic spikes. - Redis or Memcached can be used for caching to reduce server load.

mitigations.name: Integrity-Protected Control Commands and Real-Time Anomaly Detection
mitigations.description: Authenticate all therapy-related commands, validate dose/timing parameters against strict clinical limits, and run real-time anomaly detection on delivery patterns to block unauthorized stoppage, excessive dosing, or runaway stimulation caused by cyberattacks or system failures.

mitigations.name: Redundant Safety Controllers and Independent Therapy Safeguards
mitigations.description: Use independent hardware or safety controllers that enforce therapy limits, monitor for abnormal delivery patterns, and automatically enter safe fallback states—such as reverting to baseline pacing, stopping infusion, or clamping stimulation—when control logic or network inputs appear manipulated or fail.

mitigations.name: Implement information hiding techniques
mitigations.description: Use information hiding techniques to make the existence or nature of data unintelligible to unauthorized parties. Focus on methods like steganography, digital watermarking, covert channels, and data obfuscation that go beyond encryption or anonymization to conceal the presence or relevance of sensitive information.
mitigations.consideration: - Employ strong encryption methods for data at rest and in transit. - Use these techniques were appropriate: - Use steganography and watermarking to conceal data in digital media - Employ covert channels to transmit hidden data within authorized flows - Apply data obfuscation to confuse unauthorized viewers - Implement anonymizing networks (e.g., Tor) to hide user activity metadata - Add traffic padding to obscure transmission patterns and volumes
mitigations.explanation: Information hiding techniques conceal sensitive data or its existence from unauthorized viewers. Methods include steganography, digital watermarking, covert channels, and data obfuscation. Anonymizing networks hide user behavior, and traffic padding masks communication patterns. These methods adapt to evolving threats to protect privacy across various digital environments.
mitigations.example: Tor and I2P anonymize network traffic, hiding user identity and activity. - Steganographic tools Embed secret messages in media files. - watermarking software secures copyright and embeds hidden metadata. - Obfuscation libraries mix or mask sensitive data values. - VPNs and traffic padding tools obscure communication timing and size patterns.

mitigations.name: Implement unique first login credentials
mitigations.description: Use a "first login" mode that prompts users to create a unique, strong password or key instead of hard-coding default credentials.
mitigations.consideration: - Prompt users to set unique credentials during first login instead of using defaults. - Enforce password complexity rules during initial credential setup. - Deliver temporary login credentials securely (e.g., email, SMS, secure link). - Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) during first-time access. - Limit credential validity duration before first login.
mitigations.explanation: During the first login, the system generates a unique, temporary credential for the user, which is sent via a secure channel. The user is prompted to create a strong password that meets predefined complexity requirements. The temporary credential expires after a set time, and all first login attempts are logged for auditing and threat detection.
mitigations.example: - AWS IAM: Prompts new users to set a unique password instead of using default credentials. - Azure Active Directory: Enforces first-time password setup with optional MFA. - Google Cloud Identity: Uses a secure "first login" flow requiring new credential creation. - Okta: Provides customizable first login policies, including password strength and expiration.

mitigations.name: Disable or Cryptographically Lock Debug Interfaces in Production Devices
mitigations.description: Permanently disable UART, JTAG, SWD, USB-serial, and proprietary maintenance modes on production hardware—or secure them with cryptographic authentication, fuse settings, or password-protected access—so unauthorized users cannot exploit manufacturing or service interfaces to gain device control.

mitigations.name: Physical Hardening and Tamper Detection for Service Ports
mitigations.description: Obscure or seal maintenance interfaces using conformal coatings, tamper-evident enclosures, or physical port removal, and implement intrusion detection that triggers credential revocation or safe-mode operation when these ports are probed, preventing attackers with physical or insider access from leveraging hidden interfaces.

mitigations.name: Change default credentials immediately
mitigations.description: Change all default credentials for admin and user accounts immediately. Implement strong, unique passwords for each account to prevent unauthorized access.
mitigations.consideration: Identify all accounts using factory-default credentials - Change default usernames and passwords during initial setup - Use tools or scripts to Enforce password changes upon first login - Remove or Disable default accounts that are not needed - Apply secure, unique passwords when replacing default credentials - verify that no systems are deployed with hardcoded or unchanged defaults
