mitigations.description: Define and enforce maximum limits on all incoming parameters and payload sizes to prevent resource exhaustion and mitigate potential DoS attacks.
mitigations.consideration: Define input size limits for body, headers, and query parameters - Validate request size server-side before processing - Reject oversized inputs with proper HTTP error codes - Log and Monitor size-limit violations for analysis - Tune limits over time based on observed usage and threat patterns - Use WAFs or Middleware to Enforce limits as close to entry as possible
mitigations.explanation: Size-based attacks can exhaust memory or processing resources. To prevent this, configure server or middleware components to reject inputs that exceed defined limits for body, query, or headers. Requests over the threshold should return errors like HTTP 413. Logging should track repeated violations for analysis. Periodic review of usage trends and threat intelligence helps ensure that the defined limits remain appropriate and effective.
mitigations.example: AWS WAF / Cloudflare WAF: block requests exceeding size thresholds - NGINX / HAProxy: Configure max body and header sizes - Kong / Apigee: API Gateways with request size enforcement - Express.js / Django: Use Middleware to limit and Validate input sizes - Spring Boot: Supports multipart and payload size limits via config - FastAPI / Flask: allow Custom validation logic for payload constraints

mitigations.name: Evaluate service provider API security
mitigations.description: Assess the security of your service provider’s API by evaluating their authentication, encryption, and access control mechanisms. Ensure their practices align with industry standards and your application’s risk requirements. Confirm that the API supports secure transmission and handles errors gracefully.
mitigations.consideration: - Review API documentation for authentication, encryption, error handling, and rate limits. - Evaluate the provider’s API under different conditions to test reliability and performance. - Confirm compatibility with your system and review support and update policies. - Check for logging capabilities and incident response procedures. - Ensure the provider uses secure protocols (e.g., OAuth 2.0, TLS).
mitigations.explanation: Evaluating service provider API security involves reviewing documentation and conducting functional tests under real-world conditions. The goal is to ensure secure access, proper error handling, scalability, and resilience to attacks. This helps confirm that the API can be a sustainable and secure part of your architecture.
mitigations.example: Postman: for testing API functionality, rate limiting, and authentication. - OWASP ZAP: Open-source tool for scanning APIs for vulnerabilities. - AWS API gateway: Offers built-in support for authentication, throttling, and logging. - Azure API Management: Enables secure access, monitoring, and access control. - Google cloud Apigee: Provides API analytics, Policy enforcement, and threat protection.

mitigations.name: Validate and sanitize API inputs
mitigations.description: Validate and sanitize all data from integrated APIs. Implement an allowlist for redirects to ensure only trusted sources are accessed.
mitigations.consideration: Define strict schemas for accepted data formats and types. - Use regex to Validate expected patterns. - Apply output encoding to sanitize user input. - Maintain allowlists for trusted Redirect destinations. - Validate all inputs at the boundary Layer of each API.
mitigations.explanation: API input validation checks incoming data against expected schemas and patterns. Inputs are sanitized by encoding or removing unsafe characters. Allowlists restrict redirects to trusted domains. Validation is enforced at API boundaries, and results are logged for audit purposes.
mitigations.example: OWASP ZAP: detects invalid or unsafe API inputs. - Joi (Node.js) & Marshmallow (Python): Enforce strict schemas. - AWS API gateway: Validates request structure. - Azure API Management: Sanitizes and Validates inputs. - Cloudflare WAF: filters and Blocks malicious requests.

mitigations.name: Source trusted libraries and packages
mitigations.description: Source components exclusively from official repositories. Regularly audit and update libraries and frameworks to ensure they are maintained and free from vulnerabilities.
mitigations.consideration: verify the integrity of libraries using checksums or digital signatures - Use official repositories with active community and vendor support - Monitor Security advisories for components in Use - automate Dependency Management and update tracking - Establish a process for deprecating and replacing outdated libraries - limit or Review Use of third-party libraries from unknown or unverified sources
mitigations.explanation: Implement tools that source libraries from trusted repositories and verify integrity using digital signatures or checksums. Regular audits should identify outdated or risky components. Automate alerts for security advisories and enforce policies for deprecating unsupported libraries. Dependency managers help track third-party usage and reduce reliance on unverified sources, promoting safe and reliable software composition.
mitigations.example: npm: sources packages from the official Node Registry and includes Audit tools - Maven: manages Java dependencies from Maven Central with version control - Composer: Pulls PHP libraries from Packagist and includes Security advisories - GitHub Dependabot: Automates updates and Flags vulnerable packages - Snyk: Scans Open-source libraries and recommends secure alternatives - JFrog Artifactory: Hosts trusted internal and third-party components securely
